<reason>PRO won by dismantling CON's foundational premise that the sex marker is an "objective, stable, externally checkable" biological record. PRO showed the field is already revisable and self-declared in most jurisdictions, then used pressure questions to force CON into either inconsistency or a bullet-bite; CON chose the latter, admitting in [B4.1] it opposes existing marker changes too, which left CON defending a status quo that doesn't exist rather than the motion's actual comparison. PRO also demanded concrete failures from jurisdictions with years of X markers, and CON's "diffused friction" answer was plausible but evidentiarily thin against PRO's real-world track record. CON's better points (letter guides placement until overridden, convenience of dodging sex-based searches, the unconscious patient) kept it competitive and consistent, but PRO answered each function concretely and weighed more cleanly. PRO's two clipped turns are a real execution cost but lost little substance, and its A1/A2 answers were direct where CON's Q2 answer partly evaded the evidentiary ask.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Q1 [A3.1] forcing CON to choose between the "medical anchor" and the existing right to change markers, followed by CON's [B4.1] concession that it opposes all marker loosening and PRO's [A5.1] exploitation of that as a wish to roll back existing law rather than defend the actual comparison.</best_rebuttal>
